n.1: 0.09 g misplaces the decimal point; it is ten times too small even for 100 mL, let alone a liter.
n.3: 90 g would be a 9% solution; this moves the decimal point one place too far.

q: A pharmacist must prepare 200 mL of a 2 M solution by diluting a 10 M stock solution with water. What volume of the stock solution is needed? Enter your answer in milliliters as a whole number.

tr.160: Gave the volume of water to add, not the volume of stock needed.

w: Use C1V1 = C2V2 (the moles of solute do not change on dilution). 10 M x V1 = 2 M x 200 mL, so V1 = 400 / 10 = 40 mL of stock, made up to 200 mL with 160 mL of water.

q: A student adds sugar to water at 25 °C and stirs for several minutes, but some sugar crystals remain undissolved on the bottom of the glass. How should the liquid in the glass be classified?
o: Saturated, so it cannot dissolve any other solute
Unsaturated, because the stirring is not yet complete
Saturated, holding the most sugar it can at 25 °C
Supersaturated, holding more sugar than its maximum
w: A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve at that temperature; any extra stays undissolved. The leftover crystals show the sugar solution has reached its limit at 25 °C.

n.0: It is saturated, but a solution saturated with sugar can still dissolve other solutes, such as salt.
n.1: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute; undissolved crystals after thorough stirring show it cannot.
n.3: A supersaturated solution holds more than the normal maximum with no undissolved solid; it is unstable and made by careful cooling.

q: Stirring a cup of iced tea makes the added sugar dissolve faster. Which statement correctly describes what stirring changes?
o: The temperature of the tea, which raises the solubility
The solubility of sugar, so more sugar can dissolve in total
The speed of dissolving, but not the solubility of sugar
Both the solubility of sugar and the speed of dissolving
w: Stirring brings fresh solvent into contact with the solute, increasing the rate of dissolving. Solubility, the maximum amount that can dissolve, depends on temperature (and pressure for gases), not on stirring.

n.0: Stirring does not noticeably change the temperature of the tea, so it does not change solubility.
n.1: Stirring affects how fast sugar dissolves, not the total amount that can dissolve.
n.3: Stirring changes the rate only; solubility at a given temperature is fixed.

q: Red blood cells are placed in a salt solution that has a higher solute concentration than the fluid inside the cells. What happens to the cells?
o: Salt moves into the cells until they burst
Water moves out of the cells, and they shrink
Water moves both ways equally, and size holds
Water moves into the cells, and they swell
w: In osmosis, water moves across a semipermeable membrane toward the higher solute concentration. The outside solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and they shrink (crenate).

n.0: Osmosis is the movement of water, not salt; the cells lose water and shrink.
n.2: Equal movement both ways describes an isotonic solution, such as 0.9% saline.
n.3: Swelling happens in a hypotonic solution, where the outside solute concentration is lower.

q: Place pure water and three aqueous solutions, each made with 1 mole of solute per kilogram of water, in order of freezing point, starting with the highest freezing point.
o: Calcium chloride (CaCl₂) solution
Sodium chloride (NaCl) solution
Glucose solution
Pure water
w: Freezing point depression is a colligative property: the more dissolved particles, the lower the freezing point. Pure water has no solute particles (freezes at 0 °C). Glucose dissolves as 1 particle per unit, NaCl gives 2 ions, and CaCl₂ gives 3 ions, so the CaCl₂ solution has the lowest freezing point.

q: A fish tank owner wants the water to hold as much dissolved oxygen as possible. Which changes would increase the amount of oxygen gas that can dissolve in the water? Select all that apply.
o: Heating the water
Cooling the water
Lowering the air pressure above the water's surface
Raising the pressure of oxygen above the water
Stirring the water faster
w: Gases are more soluble in colder liquids, and, by Henry's law, more gas dissolves when the pressure of that gas above the liquid is higher.

n.0: Heating lowers the solubility of gases; warm water holds less oxygen.
n.2: Lowering the pressure above the water lets dissolved gas escape, as when a soda is opened.
n.4: Stirring changes how quickly gas dissolves or escapes, not the maximum amount that can dissolve.

q: Solution A has a pH of 3 and solution B has a pH of 6. How does the hydrogen ion concentration of solution A compare with that of solution B?
o: 30 times greater
1,000 times greater
3 times greater
1,000 times smaller
w: The pH scale is logarithmic: each 1-unit drop in pH is a 10-fold increase in [H⁺]. From pH 6 to pH 3 is 3 units, so A has 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000 times the hydrogen ion concentration of B.

n.0: This multiplies the 3-unit difference by 10 instead of raising 10 to the third power.
n.2: This treats the pH scale as linear (6 - 3 = 3). Each pH unit is a tenfold change.
n.3: The size of the difference is right, but the lower pH (A) has the higher [H⁺], so A is more acidic, not less.

q: A student dips strips of red and blue litmus paper into a household cleaner. The red strip turns blue, and the blue strip stays blue. What does this result show about the cleaner?
o: It is a base, with a pH below 7
It is an acid, with a pH below 7
It is a base, with a pH above 7
It is neutral, with a pH of 7
w: Bases turn red litmus blue; acids turn blue litmus red. A red strip turning blue identifies a base, and bases have a pH above 7.

n.0: It is a base, but a pH below 7 describes an acid; bases have a pH above 7.
n.1: An acid would turn the blue strip red and leave the red strip unchanged, which is the opposite of what was seen.
n.3: A neutral solution would not change the color of either litmus strip.

q: Ammonia reacts with water according to NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which substance acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base in the forward reaction, and why?
o: NH₃, because it accepts a proton from water
NH₃, because it donates a proton to water
NH₃, because it contains a hydroxide ion
H₂O, because it accepts a proton from NH₃
w: A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton (H+) acceptor. NH₃ takes an H⁺ from water and becomes NH₄⁺, so NH₃ is the base and water acts as the acid (proton donor).

n.1: Donating a proton is what an acid does. NH₃ gains a proton to become NH₄⁺.
n.2: NH₃ contains no hydroxide ion; it is a base because it accepts a proton, which is the point of the Bronsted-Lowry definition.
n.3: Water loses a proton here (becoming OH⁻), so water is the acid, not the base.

q: A lab reports that a patient's arterial blood has a pH of 7.32. How should this value be classified?
o: Alkalosis, because it is above the neutral pH of 7
Acidosis, because it is below the normal range of 7.35-7.45
Normal, because blood is slightly acidic at about 7.3
Normal, because it is within 0.5 of the neutral pH of 7
w: Normal blood pH is 7.35-7.45, which is slightly basic. A pH below 7.35 is acidosis and a pH above 7.45 is alkalosis, so 7.32 is acidosis even though it is above 7.

n.0: Blood is judged against its normal range, not against neutral 7; 7.32 is below that range, which is acidosis.
n.2: Normal blood is slightly basic (7.35-7.45), not slightly acidic, and 7.32 falls below the normal range.
n.3: The healthy range is narrow (7.35-7.45); being near 7 is not the standard for blood.

q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is described as a strong acid, while the acetic acid in vinegar is a weak acid. What does the term 'strong' refer to?
o: How completely the acid ionizes in water
How many hydrogen atoms each molecule holds
How concentrated the acid solution is
How much base is needed to neutralize it
w: Acid strength refers to the degree of ionization: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely in water, while a weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partially.

n.1: The number of hydrogen atoms does not set strength; acetic acid (CH₃COOH) has four hydrogens but is weak.
n.2: Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in a volume; a strong acid can be dilute and a weak acid concentrated.
n.3: The amount of base needed depends on the moles of acid present, not on whether the acid is strong or weak.

q: An antacid containing magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂, is taken to neutralize excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. What are the products of this neutralization reaction?
o: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas
Magnesium chloride and carbon dioxide
Magnesium chloride and water
Magnesium oxide and chlorine gas
w: Acid + base → salt + water. Mg(OH)₂ + 2 HCl → MgCl₂ + 2 H₂O: the salt is magnesium chloride, and H⁺ from the acid joins OH⁻ from the base to form water.

n.0: Hydrogen gas forms when an acid reacts with an active metal, not with a hydroxide base.
n.1: Carbon dioxide forms when an acid reacts with a carbonate antacid (such as CaCO₃); magnesium hydroxide contains no carbon.
n.3: Neutralization swaps ions to give a salt and water; it does not produce chlorine gas or an oxide.

q: The carbonic acid-bicarbonate system helps keep blood pH within its normal range. Which statement best describes how a buffer such as this one works?
o: It pairs a strong acid with a strong base in equal amounts
It makes blood neutral, holding its pH close to 7.0
It resists pH change when a little acid or base is added
It sends added acid to the kidneys for removal within seconds
w: A buffer, usually a weak acid and its conjugate base, resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added: the base part absorbs added H⁺, and the acid part neutralizes added OH⁻. Its capacity is limited.

n.0: Buffers are made from a weak acid and its conjugate base (H₂CO₃ and HCO₃⁻); a strong acid and strong base would simply neutralize each other.
n.1: Blood is kept slightly basic, at 7.35-7.45, not neutral; the buffer limits pH change around that value rather than moving it to 7.0.
n.3: The kidneys adjust H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ over hours to days; the buffer itself acts chemically and at once, binding added H⁺ with bicarbonate.

q: A cleaning solution has a pOH of 3 at 25 °C. What is the pH of the solution? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.3: Copied the pOH as the pH.

w: At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, so pH = 14 - 3 = 11. The solution is basic (pH above 7).

q: A few drops of phenolphthalein indicator are added to a clear, colorless solution, and the solution turns pink. Which of these could the solution be?
o: Distilled water
Dilute sodium hydroxide
Carbonated water
Dilute acetic acid (vinegar)
w: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions and turns pink in basic solutions. Sodium hydroxide is a strong base.

n.0: Pure water is neutral (pH 7), so phenolphthalein stays colorless.
n.2: Carbonated water contains carbonic acid, so it is acidic and the indicator stays colorless.
n.3: Vinegar is acidic, so phenolphthalein stays colorless.

q: Place these substances in order of pH, starting with the most acidic and ending with the most basic.
o: Household ammonia
Stomach acid
Black coffee
Human blood
Pure water
w: Approximate pH values: stomach acid 1.5-3.5, black coffee about 5, pure water 7 (neutral), blood 7.35-7.45 (slightly basic) and household ammonia about 11. Lower pH means more acidic.

q: A student is listing the typical properties of acids for a study guide. Which properties are characteristic of acids? Select all that apply.
o: They react with zinc to release hydrogen gas
They turn blue litmus paper red
They taste sour
They turn phenolphthalein pink
They accept protons from water molecules
They feel slippery to the touch
w: Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, and react with active metals such as zinc to release hydrogen gas (H₂). They donate protons (H+).

n.3: Phenolphthalein turns pink in bases; it stays colorless in acids.
n.4: Accepting protons defines a Bronsted-Lowry base; acids donate protons.
n.5: A slippery, soapy feel is a property of bases.

q: A 0.001 M solution of hydrochloric acid (HCl) is compared with a 1 M solution of acetic acid. Which statement correctly compares the two acids?
o: HCl is the stronger acid, because its solution is more concentrated
Acetic acid is the stronger acid, because its solution is more concentrated
HCl is the stronger acid, even though its solution is more dilute
The two are equally strong, because both release hydrogen ions
w: Strength and concentration are different ideas. HCl is a strong acid because it ionizes completely; acetic acid is weak because it ionizes only partly. Here the strong acid happens to be in the more dilute solution.

n.0: HCl is stronger, but its solution is the more dilute one (0.001 M vs 1 M).
n.1: A more concentrated solution does not make an acid stronger; acetic acid is weak at any concentration.
n.3: Both release H⁺, but HCl ionizes completely and acetic acid only partly, so they differ in strength.
